contribution: Earlier chapters have taught you to measure and to present results. This chapter puts the skills together into an experimental investigation: a question and a hypothesis, a fair experiment, choosing the measuring range on the basis of uncertainty, the lab record and the report.
learn: You can formulate a research question and a testable hypothesis.
You can plan a fair experiment: choose the variables, the measuring range and the repeats.
You can record measurements in a lab record and report a result with its uncertainty.
prior: A measurement result has an uncertainty, and repeating the measurement gives a mean (chapter *Measuring and the reliability of a measurement*)
A straight line is fitted to the data points, and its slope tells the rate of change (chapter *Graphs and fitting a straight line*)

activities.text: Two groups measure the speed of the same toy car with a hand stopwatch. Group A runs the car once over a distance of $0.50\,\text{m}$, gets a time of $1.0\,\text{s}$ and calculates a speed of $0.50\,\text{m/s}$. Group B runs five different distances, three times each. Over $2.00\,\text{m}$ the mean time is $4.73\,\text{s}$, and group B calculates a speed of $0.42\,\text{m/s}$. The car and the batteries are the same.
activities.question: Why do the results differ, and how should an investigation be designed so that its result can be trusted?

activities.title: Review: repeats and uncertainty
activities.prompt: A student measures a walking time five times and gets $4.7\,\text{s}$, $4.9\,\text{s}$, $4.6\,\text{s}$, $4.8\,\text{s}$ and $4.7\,\text{s}$. What is the most sensible way to report the result?

choices.text: $4.9\,\text{s}$, because the largest reading is the surest.
choices.feedback: A single extreme value is just one measurement among the others. When a measurement is repeated, the mean is a better estimate than the largest or smallest reading (chapter *Measuring and the reliability of a measurement*).

choices.text: $4.74\,\text{s}$ without uncertainty, because the calculator gives two decimals.
choices.feedback: The calculator gives digits that the measurement does not really know: the readings already vary by a tenth of a second. A result is given with the precision that matches the uncertainty, and together with it (chapter *Measuring and the reliability of a measurement*).

choices.text: $4.7\,\text{s} \pm 0.2\,\text{s}$: the mean, and as the uncertainty half of the range rounded up.
choices.feedback: Correct. The mean is $23.7\,\text{s} : 5 = 4.74\,\text{s} \approx 4.7\,\text{s}$ and half of the range is $(4.9\,\text{s} - 4.6\,\text{s}) : 2 = 0.15\,\text{s} \approx 0.2\,\text{s}$. Today you plan an experiment so that this uncertainty is small compared with the measurement.

choices.text: $4.7\,\text{s}$ without uncertainty, because the mean already tells everything.
choices.feedback: The mean gives the result, but not how much it can vary. Without an uncertainty no one else can judge whether the result fits a prediction or another measurement (chapter *Measuring and the reliability of a measurement*).

activities.title: Prediction: why the results differ
activities.prompt: The speed of group A is $0.50\,\text{m/s}$ and that of group B $0.42\,\text{m/s}$. What explains the difference best?

choices.text: The car of group B went more slowly over the long distance.
choices.feedback: This is a testable hypothesis, but the lab record of group B (section Investigate) does not support it: the speed of the car stays about the same even over long distances, $0.42\,\text{m/s}$. So the difference is not due to the distance but to how the time was measured.

choices.text: The speed of the car is greater over a short distance than over a long distance.
choices.feedback: This is a testable hypothesis, and you can check it by measuring several distances. The lab record of group B (section Investigate) does not support it: over the shortest distance the speed is lower, $0.39\,\text{m/s}$, not higher.

choices.text: The measured time of group A is so short that the uncertainty of the stopwatch is a large part of it.
choices.feedback: Correct. The uncertainty of the time is about $0.2\,\text{s}$, so the relative uncertainty of the time of group A is $0.2 : 1.0 = 20\,\%$ and the speed is $0.50 \pm 0.10\,\text{m/s}$. The result $0.42\,\text{m/s}$ of group B fits within this interval, and the uncertainty of B itself is only about $\pm 0.01\,\text{m/s}$. The lab record supports this.

choices.text: Because of random variation, neither result can be trusted.
choices.feedback: Random variation does not make a measurement worthless. It is estimated with an uncertainty and reduced by repeats and a longer measuring time. The result of group B is accurate to about $\pm 0.01\,\text{m/s}$, and the result of group A is very imprecise.

activities.title: Lab record of group B
activities.text:
Group B ran the car over five distances and measured three times with a hand stopwatch for each. The table shows the mean of the times $\bar{t}$, half of the range $\Delta t$, the relative uncertainty $\varepsilon = \Delta t : \bar{t}$ and the speed $v = s : \bar{t}$.

| $s\ (\text{m})$ | $t_1\ (\text{s})$ | $t_2\ (\text{s})$ | $t_3\ (\text{s})$ | $\bar{t}\ (\text{s})$ | $\Delta t\ (\text{s})$ | $\varepsilon$ | $v\ (\text{m/s})$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.50 | 1.3 | 1.1 | 1.4 | 1.27 | 0.15 | 12 % | 0.39 |
| 1.00 | 2.5 | 2.3 | 2.6 | 2.47 | 0.15 | 6.1 % | 0.41 |
| 1.50 | 3.7 | 3.5 | 3.6 | 3.60 | 0.10 | 2.8 % | 0.42 |
| 2.00 | 4.9 | 4.6 | 4.7 | 4.73 | 0.15 | 3.2 % | 0.42 |
| 2.50 | 5.8 | 6.1 | 5.9 | 5.93 | 0.15 | 2.5 % | 0.42 |

question.prompt: What can you conclude from the lab record about the speed of the car over different distances?

choices.text: The speed increases with distance, because over the shortest distance it is $0.39\,\text{m/s}$ and over the longer ones $0.42\,\text{m/s}$.
choices.feedback: The difference $0.03\,\text{m/s}$ is smaller than the uncertainty of the shortest distance: $\varepsilon = 12\,\%$ means about $\pm 0.05\,\text{m/s}$. Over the three longest distances the speed does not increase at all, so the difference does not look like a change but like scatter in the measurement.

choices.text: The speed is the same over all distances within the uncertainty, about $0.42\,\text{m/s}$. The uncertainty is greatest over the shortest distance.
choices.feedback: Correct. The value for the shortest distance, $0.39 \pm 0.05\,\text{m/s}$, includes $0.42\,\text{m/s}$, and over the longer distances the relative uncertainty is about $6\,\%$ or less. The points follow the model of uniform motion $s = vt$.

choices.text: You cannot say anything about the speed, because the three times for the same distance differ from each other.
choices.feedback: The difference between repeats does not prevent a conclusion; it is a measure of the uncertainty. Half of the range $\Delta t$ tells how much the result can vary, and you can use it to judge which differences are real.

activities.title: Distance as a function of time
activities.text: The graph shows the mean times and distances of group B. The horizontal bars of the points are the time uncertainties $\Delta t$. A straight line through the origin has been fitted to the points (chapter *Graphs and fitting a straight line*). The distance is on the vertical axis although it was the variable that was changed: the slope $\Delta s : \Delta t$ requires time to be on the horizontal axis.

question.prompt: The line passes through the origin and the point $(5.0\,\text{s};\ 2.1\,\text{m})$. What is the speed of the car, that is, the slope of the line? Give the answer in m/s.
hints: What does the slope of the graph tell you when time is on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis?
The slope is the ratio of the vertical change to the horizontal change: $v = \dfrac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}$.
The line passes through the origin, so $\Delta s = 2.1\,\text{m} - 0\,\text{m}$ and $\Delta t = 5.0\,\text{s} - 0\,\text{s}$.

mistakes.feedback: You divided the time by the distance. The slope is $\Delta s : \Delta t$, that is, distance divided by time; your answer $t : s$ is the reciprocal, with the unit $\text{s/m}$.
You read only the distance. The speed is the ratio of distance to time, so the distance $2.1\,\text{m}$ must be divided by the time $5.0\,\text{s}$.

question.solution:
**Given:** a point on the line $(t, s) = (5.0\,\text{s};\ 2.1\,\text{m})$, and the line passes through the origin $(0, 0)$

**Find:** the speed $v$ of the car in $\text{m/s}$

**Principle:** The motion of the car is uniform, so the distance is directly proportional to time, $s = vt$, and the line of the $(t, s)$ graph passes through the origin. The slope of the line is the speed.

**Reading the graph:** Read a point from the line whose coordinates are known accurately: when $t = 5.0\,\text{s}$, the line is at the height $s = 2.1\,\text{m}$. The other point is the origin. The slope is calculated between these points.

**Formula:** $v = \dfrac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{s_2 - s_1}{t_2 - t_1}$

**Conversions:** The distance is in metres and the time in seconds, so no conversions are needed.

**Substitution:** $v = \dfrac{2.1\,\text{m} - 0\,\text{m}}{5.0\,\text{s} - 0\,\text{s}} = \dfrac{2.1\,\text{m}}{5.0\,\text{s}} = 0.42\,\text{m/s}$

**Answer:** $0.42\,\text{m/s}$, two significant figures, because the distance $2.1\,\text{m}$ read from the graph can be read to two figures.

**Reasonableness:** The result agrees with the speeds $0.42\,\text{m/s}$ in the table for the longer distances. The last point of the graph gives $2.50\,\text{m} : 5.93\,\text{s} = 0.42\,\text{m/s}$, so the line describes the points well.

activities.title: A fair experiment?
activities.prompt: Group C investigates how the number of batteries affects the speed of a toy car. It first runs a new car with two batteries on the floor and then an old car with four batteries on a carpet. The speed is lower the second time. What is the most important flaw in the plan?

choices.text: Several things change at the same time: the batteries, the car and the surface. You cannot tell what caused the change in speed.
choices.feedback: Correct. In a fair experiment you change only the number of batteries and keep the car and the surface the same. Now the slowing down could be due to the carpet, the old car or the batteries, and the measurement does not separate them.

choices.text: The number of batteries should be measured and not chosen by yourself.
choices.feedback: The investigator chooses the number of batteries, because that is the thing whose effect is being investigated. What is measured is the speed of the car. The worst flaw is still that other things change as well.

choices.text: There are only two measurements, so the results cannot be compared.
choices.feedback: Two points is very few, and more values and repeats would be better. Even so, comparing two points would be sensible if the other variables were the same. The essential flaw is that the comparison is not fair.

activities.title: Return to your prediction
activities.prompt: Compare your prediction with the lab record of group B and the formula for relative uncertainty. Then return to the opening question: why do the results of group A and group B differ, and how should an investigation be designed so that its result can be trusted?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt:
A student plans an experiment in which the speed of the car is $0.60\,\text{m/s}$ and the uncertainty of the time is $0.2\,\text{s}$. The limit of the relative uncertainty is $5\,\%$. They calculate the shortest distance:

$$\begin{aligned} s_\text{min} &= \frac{v\,\Delta t}{\varepsilon_\text{max}} \\ &= \frac{0.60\,\text{m/s} \cdot 0.2\,\text{s}}{5} \\ &= 0.024\,\text{m} \end{aligned}$$

Where is the error?

choices.text: The percentage was not converted to a decimal number: $5\,\% = 0.050$, so the correct distance is $0.60\,\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} \cdot 0.2\,\text{s} : 0.050 = 2.4\,\text{m}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. The relative uncertainty $\varepsilon$ is a quotient, so $5\,\%$ must be substituted as the number $0.050$. The error could have been noticed with a reasonableness check: you cannot measure a distance of a couple of centimetres with a hand stopwatch when the time is under a second.

choices.text: The formula is wrong: the distance should be calculated by dividing the uncertainty by the speed.
choices.feedback: The formula is correct. The shortest time is $t_\text{min} = \Delta t : \varepsilon_\text{max}$ and the distance is $s = v\,t_\text{min}$. Dividing the uncertainty by the speed would give a combination of seconds and speed that has no unit of distance.

choices.text: The uncertainty should be converted to milliseconds before substituting.
choices.feedback: No conversion is needed, because the speed is in $\text{m/s}$ and the uncertainty in seconds; the seconds cancel and the result is in metres. The error is in how the percentage was handled.

activities.title: Apply to a new situation
activities.prompt: Students measure walking speed, about $1.4\,\text{m/s}$, with a hand stopwatch. The uncertainty of the time is $0.3\,\text{s}$, and the relative uncertainty must be at most $3.0\,\%$. What is the shortest valid measuring distance? Give the answer in metres.
hints: What length of time makes the relative uncertainty $3.0\,\%$ when the uncertainty is $0.3\,\text{s}$?
The shortest time is $t_\text{min} = \dfrac{\Delta t}{\varepsilon_\text{max}}$, and the percentage must be substituted as a decimal number. The distance comes from the model $s = vt$.

mistakes.feedback: You substituted the percentage as the number $3.0$ and not $0.030$. The relative uncertainty is a quotient, so $3.0\,\% = 0.030$.
You calculated only the shortest time $0.3\,\text{s} : 0.030 = 10\,\text{s}$. The distance is obtained by multiplying the time by the speed: $s = vt$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** speed $v = 1.4\,\text{m/s}$, uncertainty of the time $\Delta t = 0.3\,\text{s}$, limit of the relative uncertainty $\varepsilon_\text{max} = 3.0\,\% = 0.030$

**Find:** the shortest valid measuring distance $s_\text{min}$ in metres

**Principle:** The uncertainty of a hand stopwatch is the same in a long and a short measurement, so the relative uncertainty gets smaller as the time gets longer. Walking is approximately uniform motion, so the distance comes from the model $s = vt$.

**Formula:** $t_\text{min} = \dfrac{\Delta t}{\varepsilon_\text{max}}$ and $s_\text{min} = v\, t_\text{min} = \dfrac{v\,\Delta t}{\varepsilon_\text{max}}$

**Conversions:** The percentage is converted to a decimal number: $3.0\,\% = 0.030$. No other conversions are needed, because the time is in seconds and the speed in $\text{m/s}$.

**Substitution:** $t_\text{min} = \dfrac{0.3\,\text{s}}{0.030} = 10\,\text{s}$ and $s_\text{min} = 1.4\,\text{m/s} \cdot 10\,\text{s} = 14\,\text{m}$

**Answer:** $14\,\text{m}$, two significant figures like the speed and the limit.

**Reasonableness:** Ten seconds is 33 times the uncertainty $0.3\,\text{s}$, so the fraction is about $\tfrac{1}{33} \approx 3.0\,\%$. Fourteen metres fits in a school corridor or yard, so the experiment is feasible.

activities.title: Plan your own investigation
activities.prompt: Choose a phenomenon that you can investigate at school or at home and in which the quantities can be measured: for example the speed of walking or of a rolling ball, the cooling of water in a cup, or the stretching of a rubber band. Write a plan: research question, hypothesis, independent, dependent and controlled variables, measuring range and repeats, and how you will keep the lab record.
activities.model: Research question: how does the time a ball takes to roll depend on the distance on a level floor? The ball is always released from the same point over a short starting ramp, and timing starts when the ball passes a start line marked on the floor, by which point its speed has levelled off. Hypothesis: if the speed of the ball on the floor is approximately constant, the travel time is directly proportional to the distance, $s = vt$. If the time grows faster than the distance, the hypothesis is wrong. The independent variable is the distance from the start line (for example $1.6$–$3.2\,\text{m}$ at five equally spaced values), the dependent variable is the time with a hand stopwatch, and I keep constant the ball, the height of the ramp and the starting point, the surface and the way of starting (the ball is released without a push). In a trial run the speed of the ball is about $0.4\,\text{m/s}$. A real ball slows down slightly while rolling because of rolling resistance, so the experiment also tests whether the speed is constant enough. The uncertainty of the stopwatch is about $0.2\,\text{s}$, so over the shortest distance the time must be at least $4\,\text{s}$ for the relative uncertainty to stay at most $5\,\%$. The distance $1.6\,\text{m}$ gives a time of $4\,\text{s}$. I make three repeats for each distance and write every reading with its unit in the lab record, together with observations such as "the ball hit the wall". The trial run shows whether the distance is long enough.
criteria: The question can be measured, and the hypothesis leads to a prediction that could turn out to be wrong.
I named the independent and the dependent variable and at least two controlled variables.
I chose the measuring range, several equally spaced values and the repeats, and justified them with the uncertainty.
I described what goes in the lab record: readings, units, equipment and observations.

activities.text: **Carry out your own investigation.** Do the experiment according to your plan and keep a lab record on paper or in a spreadsheet during the measurement. Start with a trial run to check the measuring range. Then write a short report with five parts: research question and hypothesis, method, results (table and graph), discussion and conclusion. The exercises on this page are practice; the actual investigation is done with real equipment.
Practise at three levels. Level 1 exercises use one formula or reading a table, level 2 exercises have two steps or a conversion, and level 3 requires reasoning.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: Which of the following is a testable hypothesis about lubricating the axles of a toy car?

choices.text: Oil is good for the axles of a car.
choices.feedback: This is an opinion, not a hypothesis. No measurement tells what "good" means. A hypothesis must lead to a measurable prediction.

choices.text: If the axles of the car are oiled, the car travels the same distance in a shorter time than before oiling.
choices.feedback: Correct. The hypothesis predicts a measurable difference (the time gets shorter), and a measurement can show it to be wrong. In a fair experiment the car, the distance and the surface are kept the same.

choices.text: Let us investigate what happens to the axles of the car with oil.
choices.feedback: This is a topic, not a hypothesis. It has no prediction that a measurement could disprove.

choices.text: The car travels somehow differently with oil.
choices.feedback: The prediction is too loose: any result would fit it. A hypothesis must rule out some result, so that it can turn out to be wrong.

activities.title: 2. Calculating uncertainty
activities.prompt: A student measures a walking time five times: $9.8\,\text{s}$, $10.2\,\text{s}$, $10.0\,\text{s}$, $9.9\,\text{s}$ and $10.1\,\text{s}$. Half of the range is used as the uncertainty. What is the relative uncertainty of the mean as a percentage?
hints: What is the mean, and what are the largest and smallest readings?
The uncertainty is $\Delta t = \dfrac{t_\text{max} - t_\text{min}}{2}$ and the relative uncertainty $\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta t}{\bar{t}}$.

mistakes.feedback: You used the whole range $0.4\,\text{s}$ as the uncertainty. The uncertainty is half of it, $0.2\,\text{s}$.
You did not multiply the quotient by one hundred. The relative uncertainty $0.020$ is $2.0\,\%$ as a percentage.

activities.solution:
**Given:** five times $9.8\,\text{s}$, $10.2\,\text{s}$, $10.0\,\text{s}$, $9.9\,\text{s}$ and $10.1\,\text{s}$

**Find:** the relative uncertainty $\varepsilon$ of the mean as a percentage

**Principle:** The repeats give a mean, and the variation of the readings gives the uncertainty: half of the range. The relative uncertainty is the uncertainty divided by the mean.

**Formula:** $\bar{t} = \dfrac{\sum t_i}{5}$, $\Delta t = \dfrac{t_\text{max} - t_\text{min}}{2}$ and $\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta t}{\bar{t}}$

**Conversions:** All times are in seconds, so no conversions are needed. The quotient is multiplied by one hundred to get a percentage.

**Substitution:** the sum of the times is $50.0\,\text{s}$, so $\bar{t} = \dfrac{50.0\,\text{s}}{5} = 10.0\,\text{s}$ and $\Delta t = \dfrac{10.2\,\text{s} - 9.8\,\text{s}}{2} = 0.2\,\text{s}$, so $\varepsilon = \dfrac{0.2\,\text{s}}{10.0\,\text{s}} = 0.020 = 2.0\,\%$

**Answer:** $2.0\,\%$, two significant figures like the mean $10.0\,\text{s}$.

**Reasonableness:** Ten seconds is 50 times the uncertainty $0.2\,\text{s}$, so the fraction is about $\tfrac{1}{50} = 2.0\,\%$. All readings are within $0.2\,\text{s}$ of the mean, as the uncertainty is meant to describe.

activities.title: 3. Explain the conclusion
activities.prompt: The conclusion of a student's report reads: "The hypothesis was proved correct, because the measurement gave the speed $0.42\,\text{m/s}$ as predicted." Explain what is too strong in the claim and how the conclusion should be worded.
criteria: I say that one experiment does not prove a hypothesis but gives it support or refutes it.
I mention that a result has an uncertainty and that a conclusion is only as strong as the data.
I word the conclusion so that it contains the result with its uncertainty and the answer to the research question.
I mention what still needs investigating or what remained uncertain.
activities.model: One experiment cannot prove a hypothesis correct. It can give it support if the result agrees with the prediction within the uncertainty, or refute it. A conclusion must contain the result with its uncertainty, for example $v = 0.42 \pm 0.02\,\text{m/s}$, and it must be compared with the prediction: the result fits the prediction, so the measurement supports the hypothesis. It must also say under what conditions the result was obtained, for example with a particular car and surface, and what was left uninvestigated, such as longer distances. This lets someone else judge how far the conclusion can be trusted.

activities.text: Finally, three quick questions. Answer them yourself first and only then open the answer.
